title: Delegation and Verification under AI
claim: A worker's choice to delegate and verify routes the task through different paths with different payoffs, so worker and institution utilities can diverge under AI.
layout: Top-down flow chart, 3 branching rows, crossing red arrows to two utility boxes
description: A top-down flow chart with blue-header rounded boxes and clip-art icons. At the top, a task arrow enters a 'Worker thinking' box (thought cloud with gears and a question mark, 'd=?'). Branches labeled d=0 and d=1, plus a middle branch, lead to three boxes in a row: Manual work (person at a desk, success rate p_w, cost C_w), Verification (document with a magnifying glass, success rate φ(s), intensity s) and Delegate to AI (robot-human handshake, p_a, C_a). Horizontal arrows between them carry probabilities such as (1−p_a)φ(s) and 'decide effort s'. Dark blue arrows with payoff formulas run down to two bottom boxes, Worker utility U_W (the text says it increases with AI adoption) and Institution utility U_I (the text asks whether it increases or decreases). Red arrows cross in the middle to show the institution's differing valuation. The eye goes first to the top box, then down the branches.
caption: A flow chart for the workflow under AI assistance with worker action $(d,s)\in [0,1]^2$.
abstract: As AI systems enter institutional workflows, workers must decide whether to delegate task execution to AI and how much effort to invest in verifying AI outputs, while institutions evaluate workers using outcome-based standards that may misalign with workers' private costs. We model delegation and verification as the solution to a rational worker's optimization problem, and define worker quality by evaluating an institution-centered utility (distinct from the worker's objective) at the resulting optimal action. We formally characterize optimal worker workflows and show that AI induces *phase transitions*, where arbitrarily small differences in verification ability lead to sharply different behaviors. As a result, AI can amplify workers with strong verification reliability while degrading institutional worker quality for others who rationally over-delegate and reduce oversight, even when baseline task success improves and no behavioral biases are present. These results identify a structural mechanism by which AI reshapes institutional worker quality and amplifies quality disparities between workers with different verification reliability.
